exponent-rules.why: The exponent laws are not rules to memorise; they are consequences of what an exponent means. ~x^{3} \cdot x^{4}~ is three copies times four copies, so seven copies. Derive them once from counting copies and you will never mix them up.
traps: Add exponents when multiplying, subtract when dividing, multiply for a power of a power. The one thing you never do is multiply when multiplying.

zero-negative-exponents.why: ~x^{0} = 1~ and ~x^{-n} = \f{1}{x^{n}}~ are forced by the division rule, not invented. ~\f{x^{3}}{x^{3}}~ is both ~x^{0}~ and 1, so they must be equal. Continuing the pattern downward past zero produces reciprocals.
traps: A negative exponent never makes a negative answer. ~2^{-3} = \f{1}{8}~, not -8.

scientific-notation.why: Scientific notation separates a number's digits from its size, which is how science and engineering handle quantities spanning forty orders of magnitude. Exactly one non-zero digit sits before the point.
traps: ~0.4 \times 10^{5}~ is not in scientific notation — the number part must be at least 1 and under 10.

sci-notation-arithmetic.why: Handle the number parts and the powers separately: multiply the fronts and add the exponents, or divide the fronts and subtract. Then renormalise if the front has drifted outside 1 to 10.
traps: Adding and subtracting needs the *same* exponent first. ~3\times10^{5} + 4\times10^{3}~ is not ~7\times10^{8}~.

radicals-simplify.why: Simplifying a root means pulling out the largest perfect square. ~sqrt{72} = sqrt{36 \cdot 2} = 6sqrt{2}~. Exact form matters because it stays exact — rounding early compounds error through a long calculation.
traps: ~sqrt{a+b}~ is not ~sqrt{a} + sqrt{b}~. Test it: ~sqrt{9+16} = 5~ but ~3 + 4 = 7~.

rational-irrational.why: Rational means expressible as a ratio of whole numbers; everything else is irrational. Terminating and repeating decimals are rational; ~sqrt{2}~ and ~\pi~ are not. The distinction is what tells you when an answer can be exact.
traps: A rational plus an irrational is always irrational, but an irrational times an irrational can be rational: ~sqrt{2} \times sqrt{2} = 2~.
